artworks.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
artworks.description: Rubens' Prado sketch for the Torre de la Parada shows the flood survivors casting stones that become a new human race — Ovid's Metamorphoses staged as Baroque energy after the waters fall. Deucalion and Pyrrha kneel among wreckage while earth repopulates behind them.

artworks.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
artworks.description: Castiglione's Denver Art Museum canvas isolates the couple in a rocky waste as they throw their 'mother's bones' — the stones of earth — that rise as men and women. The Genoese painter makes the Greek flood myth a study of survival and second creation.

artworks.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
artworks.description: Solis's woodcut for Ovid's Metamorphoses freezes the oracle's command: husband and wife hurl stones over their shoulders while new bodies form from the ground. The print carried Deucalion's flood into countless Renaissance editions of the poem.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Book 1 makes Deucalion and Pyrrha the survivors who repopulate the world from stones — the Greek flood told as Rome's foundational metamorphosis.

popCulture.title: Deucalion
popCulture.description: Son of Prometheus, husband of Pyrrha — the Hellenic Noah whose name still marks flood myths and the Deucalionid line of Hellen.
